newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire conflict forces some refugees into Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Zaire conflict forces some refugees into Rwanda.

text.p: The spreading conflict in eastern Zaire has convinced some Rwandan refugees to return to the homeland they fled in fear two years ago, aid workers said on Sunday.
Warfare between ethnic Tutsi rebels and Zairean government troops has forced about half a million Rwandan Hutus to flee refugee camps just inside eastern Zaire.
Most have trekked deeper into Zaire but aid workers said several thousand were crossing over to Rwanda, where refugees have feared persecution or punishment for genocide crimes.

More than one million Rwandan Hutu refugees have lived in a string of camps in eastern Zaire since 1994. They fled Rwanda fearing reprisals for the 1994 genocide in which Hutus killed up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Michele Quintaglie of the World Food Programme said that about 1,500 Rwandans had crossed into Rwanda from Zaire and were now at the Nkamira waystation near the town of Gisenyi.
Quintaglie, speaking by telephone from the Ugandan capital Kampala, said about 3,000 Zaireans had also fled to Rwanda.
Quintaglie, in telephone contact with the border region, said all were clearly fleeing serious fighting.
"There are nine Zairean refugees who are wounded. Five are reported to be heavily wounded," she said.

Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees in the Rwandan capital Kigali, said earlier that at least 5,000 Rwandan refugees fled into Rwanda on Sunday morning at the border post of Mutura.
But most of the Rwandan refugees preferred to head west.
A stream of about 200,000 fled westward after one of eastern Zaire's biggest camps was reported to have been shelled from Rwanda on Saturday and several refugees were killed.
"There is a stream of people about 25 km (15 miles) long...I saw pregnant women, handicapped people, little children," U.N. official Panos Moumtzis said from the Zairean town of Goma.
Moumtzis, another UNHCR spokesman, told Reuters that refugees said sustained artillery attacks on the Kibumba camp had come from the direction of Rwanda.

"We saw four dead bodies in Kibumba, but refugees told us there were a lot more dead...We were told there were at least 100 wounded," said Moumtzis, who visited the now abandoned camp 25 km (15 miles) north of Goma on Sunday morning.
"One of the mortars hit Kibumba hospital. They told us there were a lot of patients inside and it was absolute chaos," he said.
The refugees are on the move after a series of attacks by Tutsi rebels fighting Zairean troops in eastern Zaire.

The Tutsi rebels, from the 300,000-strong Banyamulenge community that migrated 200 years ago from what are now Rwanda to Zaire, accuse Zaire of denying them citizenship and harassment to make them leave.
The armies of both Rwanda and Burundi, Zaire's small neighbours to the east, are dominated by the Tutsi minorities and diplomats fear they are being drawn into the conflict.

A central objective for both countries is the closure of the Hutu refugee camps located right on their borders and used as bases for Hutu rebel infiltrators. This objective is being achieved by the past fortnight's fighting.
Zaire says Rwanda is sending troops to support Tutsi rebels, a charge Rwanda denies.

Moumtzis said the refugees who had fled Kibumba were being directed to a camp at Mugunga 13 km (eight miles) west of Goma. "About 5,000 refugees an hour are entering Mugunga," he said, adding that U.N. staff with loudspeakers were telling refugees not to enter Goma city.
The Zairean government closed the airport of Goma on Sunday without explanation, stranding 22 aid workers who had intended to fly out because of worsening security in eastern Zaire, Quintaglie said.
From Bukavu, a 27-seater plane evacuated French and Italian nationals, including diplomats, aid workers and civilians, without incident on Sunday.
Bukavu was tense as the sound of distant cannon fire from the south echoed round the town, and Zairean troops, recently reinforced, were noticeably nervous.
